prize_parts.citation: for the discovery and theory of collective motion and long-range order in active matter

statement.case_for: I keep active matter and flocking (B006) first. The Vicsek model gave a minimal self-propelled-particle system with a genuine nonequilibrium transition to collective motion. Toner and Tu then showed by dynamical renormalization that true long-range orientational order survives in two dimensions, which the Mermin-Wagner theorem forbids in equilibrium, and Ramaswamy's hydrodynamics of active fluids and orientational order extended the framework to active fluids. This is a new conceptual class of nonequilibrium statistical physics, not a technique. It has been tested for three decades in simulations, vibrated granular layers, bacterial suspensions and colloidal swimmers, and it reaches biology, soft matter and robotics. The three names map onto three distinct decisive contributions: a numerical model and its transition, a continuum field theory with exact-looking scaling, and a hydrodynamic description of active fluids. I weigh this on what the work taught us, not on how many colleagues put it high.
statement.case_against: My own ballot is the least supported on the table: only I ranked B006 among the shortlist, and I should say plainly that this tells the Committee something. The strongest reservations are real. Quantitative confirmation of the Toner-Tu exponents is much weaker than qualitative confirmation, and the order of the Vicsek transition (continuous versus discontinuous, with strong finite-size effects) was disputed for years. The cutoff at three is contestable, since Marchetti, Cates, Simha, Chate and others have strong claims to the broader field. Against that, B024 and B003 have far wider opening support, and B024 in particular has a localized, quantitative, independently reproduced result. If the Committee judges that the decisive test of a Nobel discovery is a sharp measurable outcome, B024 is the stronger candidate than mine.

responses.point: Johansson ranks the optical lattice clock (B024) first: Katori proposed the magic-wavelength lattice and Ye drove it to the 1e-18 level, so two-person credit is clean, the result is confirmed across many laboratories, and the 2005 prize for the frequency comb makes this a timely successor.
responses.response: I agree that the attribution is clean and that the performance is independently reproduced, and I ranked it seventh mainly on a field-distance basis, not on a defect I can identify. My qualification is about novelty relative to precedent: the 2005 comb prize supplies the enabling tool and the 2012 ion-clock prize already honoured the idea of better clocks through trapping and control. The citation therefore needs to say precisely what is new, namely Doppler- and recoil-free interrogation of many atoms at a magic wavelength, and not just 'a better clock'. If that distinction can be drafted crisply, I would not oppose B024 and regard it as my first alternative on the merits of its clarity.

responses.point: Danielsson ranks magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene (B003) first as an original discovery of new phases tuned by a geometric angle, confirmed by many groups, while noting that the first-author experimentalist is omitted and the pairing mechanism is unsettled.
responses.response: I share the view that the discovery is original and that moire quantum matter is a real field, and I placed B003 third. But the two caveats Danielsson lists are, to me, close to disqualifying for a prize now, not a footnote. If the superconducting pairing and the nature of the correlated states are unsettled, the lasting-consequence test is not yet met and the credit question (Cao and the first 2018 papers versus the group leader) cannot be settled on the record. The magic-angle prediction by Bistritzer and MacDonald is on firmer ground than the interpretation of the experiments. I would ask whether a more mature statement of the discovery could be written in five or ten years, and I do not see the same drift in B006, whose core claims have been stable since the mid-1990s.

responses.point: Eriksson ranks the Car-Parrinello method (B058) first: a single 1985 scheme joining density-functional electronic structure with atomic motion, used almost universally for four decades, with an unambiguous two-name attribution.
responses.response: I ranked B058 sixth and I accept the attribution and the maturity argument entirely; there is no doubt that the method changed practice. My reservation is the category. The 1998 chemistry prize recognized density-functional theory, and the Committee has generally been more reluctant to award methods whose principal impact is in chemistry and materials computation than discoveries or instruments in physics. That is a judgement about the prize's remit, not about quality, and I would like the Committee to say explicitly which view it takes. I would also place it on a par with B006 as a theory-and-method contribution, so I do not regard it as stronger than my choice.

responses.point: Kroll ranks B024 first for its clean two-person attribution and ranks B003 fourth, noting that the microscopic origin of the superconductivity is still debated and that recognition could be somewhat early.
responses.response: I agree with the caution on B003 and think it supports mine above. Where I differ is on how much weight to put on opening ties at the top: four first-place votes for B024 reflect a shared preference for a localized, quantitative result, and I do not read it as evidence that other candidates are weak. I would ask Kroll whether the many-body, spin-polarized clock work he credits to Ye belongs in the citation, because that determines whether the prize honours the lattice-clock invention alone or also the later precision programme.

uncertainties: Whether the Committee wants a statistical-physics prize for active matter, and whether the three names Toner, Ramaswamy and Vicsek are the right cutoff against Marchetti, Cates, Simha and Chate.
Whether the quantitative confirmation of Toner-Tu scaling, as opposed to the qualitative picture, is sufficient for a lasting-consequence judgement.
How the Committee should treat novelty of B024 relative to the 2005 and 2012 prizes.
Whether the open credit and interpretation questions in B003 will settle soon enough to alter the ranking.
statement.conflict_note: No specific personal or institutional conflict is apparent from the provided profile. My field (stochastic and complex-systems physics, including active matter) is scientifically close to B006, but I have no documented collaboration, supervision or institutional tie to Toner, Ramaswamy or Vicsek, nor to the other named candidates; the Committee may wish to note the field proximity.
